summary: The Supreme Court held 6-3, in an opinion by Justice Kagan, that police acquisition of a person's cell-phone Location History data from Google via a geofence warrant is a Fourth Amendment search, rejecting the government's third-party-doctrine argument. The Court vacated the Fourth Circuit's judgment and remanded for further proceedings on whether the specific warrant satisfied the particularity and probable-cause requirements. The case originated from a 2019 credit union robbery investigation in Midlothian, Virginia. The Court did not rule on ALPRs or Flock Safety.
whyItMatters: This is the clearest signal yet that the Supreme Court will extend Fourth Amendment protection to location data held by third parties, rejecting a narrow reading of the third-party doctrine. It doesn't decide the ALPR question, but it's the doctrinal foundation ALPR challenges are now building on.
